How the diagnostics are defined

Source: vignettes/definitions.Rmd
definitions.Rmd

This vignette gives the exact definitions behind propensity_sensitivity(). Every diagnostic uses the covariates and the treatment only; none uses the outcome. These diagnostics have been studied in the author’s simulations and benchmark analyses; a methods paper is in preparation. No peer-reviewed evaluation exists yet, and no thresholds for a “large” value exist yet.

The summaries and their labels

Every summary is study-level: it describes the study as a whole. The per-patient values behind them (the patients table and as.data.frame()) describe how a summary is spread over the patients; they are not flags for individual patients. The same label is used wherever a summary appears (printed output, summary(), the articles).

Summary Label Level Row of summary$table
Rank disagreement primary study mean_rank_disagreement_treated
Rank disagreement, equal weight per algorithm exploratory study mean_rank_disagreement_equal_weight_treated
Between/within-algorithm ratio exploratory study median_between_within_ratio_treated
Pair instability exploratory study pair_instability_models_mean_treated
Bootstrap rank instability of the logistic model descriptive study bootstrap_rank_instability_treated
Balance spread (range of the largest SMD on main terms) descriptive study smd_max_main_range
Other balance spreads (extended terms, energy distance, KS) descriptive study *_range, *_sd
Control spread (scaled) descriptive study mean_control_spread_scaled_treated
Pair recurrence (across models, across bootstrap refits) descriptive study pair_recurrence_*
Logit disagreement descriptive study mean_logit_disagreement_treated
Share of treated kept descriptive study treated_kept_share, treated_kept_share_min

The names of a few columns keep the word “control” for the untreated partner (for example control_spread, distinct_controls); the text calls it the untreated partner.

Notation

Symbol Meaning
n number of patients
T_i treatment, 1 = treated, 0 = untreated
m one propensity model: one algorithm with one seed
e_m(i) cross-fitted probability of treatment from model m, clipped to [0.001, 0.999]
l_m(i) logit of e_m(i)
r_m(i) percentile rank of l_m(i) among all n patients (rank divided by n, so 0 to 1)
c_m(i) the untreated partner matched to treated patient i under model m

The model set and the quality gate

The default set of propensity_sensitivity() and of fit_propensity_models() has logistic regression (main effects), Bayesian additive regression trees (dbarts::bart2, probit link, default priors, 75 trees, four chains of 500 burn-in and 500 kept draws, posterior mean probability) and a generalized random forest (grf::probability_forest, 2,000 honest trees), the two tree algorithms with three seeds each: seven models.

A faster set is available with algorithms = c("logistic_regression", "random_forest", "gradient_boosting"): a random forest (500 trees, mtry = floor(sqrt(p)), node size 10) and gradient boosting (depth 3, shrinkage 0.05, bagging fraction 0.8; the number of trees chosen once by 5-fold cross-validation and then frozen). It has been studied less than the default set.

Every score is cross-fitted: the patients are split into five folds shared by all models, and each patient’s score comes from a model fitted on the other four folds. In-sample tree scores are overfit; cross-fitting keeps every model honest. (cross_fit = FALSE gives the in-sample scores that MatchIt would use.)

Seeds. The fold split and every tree model come from one number, seed; seeds = 1:k only sets how many tree models per algorithm are fitted. A model’s random stream also depends on its position in the list of models, so random_forest_1 is a different fit with and without logistic regression in algorithms. On small data the kept models and every summary can change noticeably with seed. Rerun with two or three values of seed and report all of them; seed_sensitivity() does this.

A model is kept only if

cross-fitted log-loss  <=  1.05 x (best model's log-loss)
max |SMD| on main terms after matching  <=  (best model's max |SMD| on main terms) + 0.10
max |SMD| on main terms after matching  <=  0.25

This is the default relative balance rule (balance_rule = "relative"): a model is excluded only when its balance is clearly worse than the best model’s. With a few hundred matched pairs the largest chance SMD over several covariates often exceeds 0.10, so a fixed 0.10 limit would exclude good models. The fixed limit is available as balance_rule = "absolute" (balance_threshold = 0.10).

If fewer than two models pass, there is no set of similarly good models to compare: every model is used, quality_gate_left_fewer_than_two_models is TRUE, and the function raises an R warning that print() repeats. If the kept models are seeds of a single algorithm, rank disagreement and pair instability measure only that algorithm’s seed noise; the function raises a second R warning, and kept_algorithms_count is 1.

The gate and the share of treated kept. With a caliper, a model that keeps few treated patients can reach an easy balance and then set the relative limit for the others. The gate does not look at the share kept by default; print() shows the share kept by each kept model. The option min_treated_kept (off by default) makes a model that keeps a smaller share fail the gate before the relative limit is computed.

Matching and the estimand

Every model is used for 1:1 nearest-neighbour matching for the average treatment effect in the treated (ATT), on the logit, by calling MatchIt::matchit() with the logit as a numeric distance. The order is MatchIt’s default for the ATT (treated patients with the largest score first). Both matching with and without replacement are supported.

Without replacement (the default of the formula interface and the more common applied choice) the result depends on the matching order, and late matches can be poor when untreated patients are not much more numerous than treated ones, so the matched estimate can keep some bias for the ATT. With replacement every treated patient gets its nearest untreated patient; under overlap and a correctly specified propensity model this targets the ATT, at the price of reused untreated patients and a variance that must account for it. With a caliper, treated patients without an eligible partner are dropped and the estimand is the effect in the retained treated patients, not the ATT.

Rank disagreement (primary) 

d(i) = standard deviation over the kept models m of r_m(i)
rank disagreement = mean of d(i) over treated patients

Percentile ranks are used rather than logits because algorithms are calibrated differently: a random forest and a logistic regression can order the patients the same way while their logits differ a lot. Ranks do not change under any increasing transformation of a score, so only the ordering of the patients counts.

logit <- c(-2, -1, 0.5, 3)
rank(logit) / 4
#> [1] 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00
rank(exp(logit)) / 4    # an increasing transformation: same ranks
#> [1] 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00

It depends on the mix of seeds. d(i) is a standard deviation over models, so its value depends on how many seeds each algorithm contributes: with the same two algorithms, more seeds of one of them pull d(i) towards that algorithm’s seed noise. Values are comparable only between runs with the same model set and the same kept algorithms.

Which treated patients each summary uses. Rank disagreement uses every treated patient, matched or not; pair instability and control spread use the treated patients matched by at least one kept model.

Rank disagreement with equal weight per algorithm, and the ratio (exploratory) 

d_between(i) = SD over algorithms a of (mean over the seeds k of a of r_{a,k}(i))
d_within(i)  = sqrt( mean over algorithms with at least two seeds of
                     (variance over seeds k of r_{a,k}(i)) )

Rank disagreement, equal weight per algorithm is the mean of d_between(i) over treated patients: each algorithm enters once, as the mean rank over its seeds, however many seeds it has. It is NA when only one algorithm is kept.

The between/within-algorithm ratio is the median over treated patients of d_between(i) / d_within(i): disagreement between algorithms divided by disagreement between seeds of the same algorithm. With three seeds per algorithm, seed noise alone gives a ratio of about 0.4; larger values point to disagreement between algorithms beyond seed noise. It is NA when no kept algorithm has two seeds. The two are not a decomposition of d(i) (d(i)^2 is not d_between(i)^2 + d_within(i)^2). Logistic regression has a single model and no seed variance, so it is left out of d_within. Standard deviations use the n − 1 denominator.

The logit-scale version d_logit(i) = SD over m of l_m(i) is descriptive.

Pair recurrence and pair instability 

pair recurrence, across models:     share of the kept models whose untreated partner equals
                                    i's most common untreated partner
pair instability (exploratory):     1 - mean over treated of the pair recurrence across models
pair recurrence, across bootstrap:  share of bootstrap refits of the logistic model that choose
                                    i's most common untreated partner, counting only refits
                                    that contain both i and that partner

Pair recurrence across models lies between 1 / (number of kept models) and 1, so pair instability lies between 0 and 1 - 1 / (number of kept models); print() shows that maximum. Pair instability is high whenever many untreated patients have similar scores, even when the models agree almost perfectly. It does not by itself mean the matched groups differ; a different partner with the same characteristics is harmless. It depends on the number of kept models and on how dense the untreated patients are, so read it next to rank disagreement, never alone. Rank disagreement and pair instability answer the same question from two sides: where untreated patients are sparse a patient’s rank can move a lot while its nearest untreated patient stays the same, and where they are dense a small move changes it.

Without the denominator correction the bootstrap version could never exceed about 0.63, because any patient is missing from about 37 % of bootstrap samples.

Bootstrap rank instability (descriptive)

The logistic model (the formula as written) is refitted in-sample on bootstrap_samples row bootstrap samples; the original patients are ranked by each refit, and the standard deviation of a patient’s rank over the refits is averaged over treated patients. It describes the sampling noise of one model, not the choice between models; report it next to rank disagreement. A sample with fewer than 10 treated or 10 untreated patients is skipped, with a message.

The bootstrap scores are not clipped by default, while the cross-fitted scores are clipped to [0.001, 0.999]. Under near-separation many cross-fitted scores can share the clipped value (tied ranks) while their bootstrap ranks stay distinct, so the two rank summaries are then not the same quantity. clip_bootstrap = TRUE clips the bootstrap scores in the same way; the default keeps the method as it was studied.

Balance spread (descriptive)

After matching on each model, four balance statistics are computed with cobalt: the maximum absolute standardized mean difference on main terms, the same with squares and all two-way interactions, the energy distance, and the maximum Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. Standardized differences use the standard deviation of the treated group, and binary covariates are standardized too, so all covariates are on one scale. The spread is the range and the standard deviation of each statistic across the kept models, with the worst model named. Report the main-terms range: with many covariates the extended-terms maximum is usually driven by sparse squares and interactions and can be large even when every main term is well balanced.

Under a caliper the standardized mean differences compare the matched treated patients with their matched untreated partners, while the energy distance (estimand = "ATT") also measures the distance to the whole treated group, so it also grows when treated patients are dropped.

Control spread (descriptive)

Different partner identities are harmless if the untreated partners have the same covariates. Control spread describes whether the models pick different kinds of untreated partners:

C(i)        = the distinct untreated partners matched to treated patient i across the models
s(i)        = mean pairwise Mahalanobis distance between the covariate vectors in C(i),
              with the covariance matrix of all n patients
s_scaled(i) = s(i) / (mean over treated patients of the Mahalanobis distance between a
                      treated patient and its logistic-regression match)

s(i) = 0 when every model picks the same untreated partner. s_scaled = 1 reads “the candidate partners differ from each other as much as a typical match differs from its treated patient”. The scale uses the logistic regression match even when logistic regression is not kept (print() names it); when that scale is 0, s_scaled is NA. Factor covariates are expanded to dummies; constant and linearly dependent columns are dropped.

Traps this design avoids

Trap What the package does
In-sample tree scores are overfit and shrink overlap all scores are cross-fitted
Random-forest out-of-bag probabilities can be exactly 0 or 1 probabilities are clipped to [0.001, 0.999] before the logit
Boosting re-tuned on every fit is not a fixed model the tree count is chosen once and frozen
Logit-scale disagreement is large even when every model orders patients alike percentile ranks are primary
Seed noise looks like model dependence equal weight per algorithm and the between/within ratio are reported; a kept set from one algorithm raises a warning
The result depends on seed seed_sensitivity() reruns with several seeds
Different partner identities need not mean different kinds of untreated partners control spread uses covariate distances
Pair recurrence is often near its floor when untreated patients are dense pair instability is reported with its maximum, as an exploratory summary next to rank disagreement, never alone
The bootstrap is not valid for the variance of matching estimators the bootstrap is used for design stability only, never for a confidence interval
No outcome-free check can tell harmful from harmless misspecification stated as a limitation: a small value is not evidence that the estimate is unbiased
